text: The site manager says the job began as a routine check and nothing more. Once he was up on the scaffolding, he noticed a roof tile that had worked loose near the gable end. The roofer with him saw rather more than that: a thin crack running under the render, all but invisible from the yard below. They called the owner in, she says, and the owner insisted on a full survey before anyone touched the wall. The bricklayer brought in to help reports scraping the face back with a trowel and uncovering mortar so crumbly that the rain had washed the life out of it. The timber frame underneath, by his account, had come through unharmed. The men then packed the wall out with a mix of sand and lime, and bedded the roof covering back down. The owner reckons the front will hold now without any special watching.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)

text: Once the stone beds lying near the building sites had been worked right out, the builders had no choice but to think their craft through again. Brick took over, and it did so on its own merits: lighter to lift, and burnt within reach of the wall it would become. The shape of the buildings shifted with it. Walls grew slimmer, openings spread wider, and the vault gave way to ceilings carried on beams. Since brick took damp badly, it was given a lime coat that let it breathe without holding the wet against the face. The trade moved too. A mason now had to read the burning of a batch rather than judge the grain of a quarried block. What came of that change was a way of building quicker to raise and cheaper to pay for, yet more easily hurt by water. The older buildings carry the mark of it still.

units: the breaking of a poured floor almost always has a traceable origin

text: A poured concrete floor hardly ever splits without a cause you can trace. The ground beneath it shifts, settles more on one side than the other, and the load stops being shared evenly. A crack opens, hair fine at first, then wider as damp works in and swells the steel bars set inside the slab. Diagnosis starts with the width of the opening, read off a gauge glued across it and checked at set intervals. Where the reading holds steady, the repair stays on the surface: cut the crack out to a taper, blow the dust away, and fill it with a resin that sets cold. Where the reading grows, the fault lies in the ground rather than the concrete, and a binder has to be injected under the footing to even out the bearing. Skip that and you will be dressing the same wound for years, because the ground keeps giving way under the patch.

text: The craftsman who took on the old farm building accepted the work out of curiosity as much as anything. On his first walk round he found two ways of building stacked in a single wall. The lower courses, laid by older hands, set uneven stones in a fat mortar, soft and almost alive under the thumb. The upper part, added long afterwards, held rigid blocks locked in grey cement. Where the base had taken up every movement of the ground without complaint, the later work had torn itself open in a good many places. He understood that the weakness lay not in the oldest material but in the ill judged marriage of two opposing logics. His advice was to take the newer section down and raise it again in a binder close to the old one. The owner wavered for a good while, and then agreed to the outlay.

text: Before you set about rendering an old wall, put the whole of your kit together: a barrow, a bucket, a wide trowel, a float and a sieve. Then see to the background itself. Rake out the hollow patches, brush the dust off, and damp the face down without soaking it. Now mix. Tip the sand into the barrow, work the lime in a little at a time, add the water, and turn it until you have a paste soft enough to spread yet stiff enough to sit on the blade. Lay it on in three passes. The first keys into the wall, the second fills the hollows, the third brings the whole face level. Let each coat dry out of the draught before you start the next. Finish by looking after the kit. Rinse the tools straight away, empty the barrow, keep the bag of lime in a dry store, and sheet the sand heap over.

text: Up on the old quarter job, the week got off to a rough start. The lads turned up to find the scaffold sitting all skew, since one windy night had been enough to shove it out of true. So it all came down again, two full days of it, and nobody grumbled. Next morning, clearing out the loft, an apprentice came across a hatch that had been sealed up under the rafters. The old hands round here had heard tell of it and never much believed it. The architect came out, stopped the demolition there and then, and the whole job swung over to saving what was left. Since then folk from the street drop by of an evening for a look at the black hole we have opened, and two neighbours even bring the men something to drink. The boss just grins. He meant to hand it over quickly, and he knows now it will be a good deal later, but it does not bother him.

text: Seen from the yard, the house looks sound enough. The pale front, the straight gable and the shutters all in line put a visitor at ease. Inside tells another tale. Under the loft the floorboards have buckled, because a split gutter has been tipping its water against the wall for seasons on end. The damp reached the timbers, lifted the render off in sheets, and left a brown ring that widens with every downpour. Lower down, the hall slab rings hollow: the sand that bedded it has been carried off by the water working through. The owners painted over the mark first, hoping to see the back of it, and the paint blistered before the next season was out, showing a background soaked right through. The survey ends plainly. Start at the roof, or everything mended below will go again before the work is done.

units: the writer finds the spread of fronts without grain worrying

text: Our streets are being clad in smooth fronts that age badly, and that ought to worry us. A wall sealed in cement no longer breathes. It traps the wet, pins it against the stone, and in the end bursts the stone from within. We have taken keeping water out for looking after a building. The cure calls for no great feat. Go back to binders that let vapour pass, keep cement for what sits below ground, and allow a face to weather instead of demanding that it stay untouched. The trades need teaching again as well, for reading an old wall is a slow discipline that the rush of the modern site has all but rubbed out. A wall rendered as it should be lasts generations on a coat of limewash and nothing more. We would rather redo every ten years what those before us got right the first time.

text: The roofing chargehand on this job learnt her trade from an old boy who never drew a line. She likes to set the two schools side by side. He laid a tile by eye, corrected the pitch as he walked the slope, and told whether it was tight by the sound of rain on it. She measures first, notes the falls, and sets the coursing out on paper before she goes up. He went up and down all day with a barrow, while she makes her loads up on the ground and lifts them in one. On one count, though, she grants him the better of it: he could feel the tiredness of a roof frame through his boots, and no set of readings takes the place of that. So she has kept his habit of pacing a roof over before she lays a hand on it. Calculation and touch run together in her work, and her jobs take less time than they did at the outset, losing nothing in strength.

text: The reworking of this market hall invites a measured verdict, best set out under three headings. The first is structure. The carpenters kept the original trusses and doubled them up without fuss, which deserves praise, since the span still reads from one end of the building to the other. The second heading is the finishing, and here the warmth cools. The render chosen is too hard, and has already opened at the bearings, while the slab, poured in one piece, takes no account of what the ground beneath it does. The third heading is use. The place is a pleasure to cross, the route through it stays clear, and the sound has been tamed without a single showy panel on view. One regret does remain: the loft is kept for the work teams alone, which denies the public the finest view of the vault.
